title: Bull Flag
teaches: The bull flag as we trade it: a leader above the 200-day and a rising 50-day makes a fast pole, rests a few sessions in a quiet drift that holds the 21-day EMA, and is bought at market when a trigger level trades, with the stop a few cents under the day's low, a third off at 3R and 5R, the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop as the planned cost.

facts.quote: A flag is a small rectangle pattern that slopes against the previous trend.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag is a small rectangle sloping against the prior trend.

facts.quote: Flags and pennants require evidence of a sharp advance or decline in heavy volume.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag needs a sharp advance on heavy volume before it.

facts.quote: The flagpole is the distance from the first resistance or support break to the high or low of the flag/pennant.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: the flagpole runs from the first break to the flag's high.

facts.quote: Ideally, these patterns will form between one and four weeks.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: ideally a flag forms in one to four weeks.

facts.quote: An expansion of volume on the resistance (support) break lends credence to the validity of the formation
facts.claim: ChartSchool: rising volume on the break adds credence.

facts.quote: Once a flag is over 12 weeks old, it would be classified as a rectangle.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag older than 12 weeks is a rectangle.

facts.quote: The flagpole which leads to the flag should be unusually steep and last several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the flagpole should be unusually steep and last several days.

facts.quote: If you don't have a straight-line (or a quick move) price run (the flagpole), then you don't have a flag.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: no straight-line run, no flag.

facts.quote: Looks like a small rectangle often tilted against the prevailing price trend.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a flag looks like a small rectangle tilted against the trend.

facts.quote: Flags are short, less than 3 weeks long. Patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags are under 3 weeks; longer patterns are rectangles or channels.

facts.quote: Downward trend 74% (up breakouts) to 77% (down breakouts) of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: volume trends down inside a flag 74% of the time for up breakouts.

facts.quote: The best performance comes when the inbound trend is upward leading to a flag which tilts downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the best flags tilt down after an upward trend.

facts.quote: A tight flag performs better than a loose one.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a tight flag performs better than a loose one.

facts.quote: A loose flag is one in which price meanders, pokes outside the trendline boundary, contains white space, or looks jagged.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a loose flag meanders, pokes outside its lines and looks jagged.

facts.quote: Look for a near vertical price run, preferably lasting several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: a near vertical run lasting several days.

facts.quote: Near the top of the flagpole, price consolidates and usually trends downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: the pause near the top usually trends down.

facts.quote: Buy when price pierces a flag or pennant trendline (D in the figure to the right) or rises above the event pattern's high (A), but not before.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: buy the trendline pierce or the move above the pattern's high, not before.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months comes first.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly pullback with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price "surfs" the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: I don't find it as effective and more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective.

facts.quote: You should sell 1/3 to 1/2 of the position after 3-5 days, and then move the stop to break even.
facts.claim: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves the stop to breakeven.

facts.quote: The rest of the position should be trailed with the 10- or the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: they tend to move in stair steps. Meaning they will make a 20-50%+ move, pull back and go sideways for a while, then make another move.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: leaders move in stair steps: a move, a sideways rest, another move.

facts.quote: day before breakout should be narrow range day or negative day
facts.claim: Bonde: the day before the breakout should be a narrow-range or down day.

facts.quote: volume on breakout day should be higher
facts.claim: Bonde: breakout-day volume should be higher.

facts.quote: stock should close near high on breakout day
facts.claim: Bonde: the breakout day should close near its high.

facts.quote: High tight flags and bull flags are the most common continuation patterns on highly ranked stock by 65 day momentum.
facts.claim: Bonde: flags are the most common continuation patterns on momentum leaders.

facts.quote: Many of these powerful momentum movers have very shallow corrections before they continue onward.
facts.claim: Bonde: momentum movers often correct very shallowly before continuing.

facts.quote: Many times the stock will form bull flag so late in the move that you would miss bulk of the possible returns by waiting for the bull flag.
facts.claim: Bonde: a flag can form so late in a move that waiting for it misses most of the return.

facts.quote: They are typically seen right after a big, quick move.
facts.claim: Zanger: flags come right after a big, quick move.

facts.quote: Bullish flags are characterized by lower tops and lower bottoms, with the pattern slanting against the trend. But unlike wedges, their trend lines run parallel.
facts.claim: Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms, slanting against the trend, with parallel lines.

facts.quote: Volume generally contracts during the pause with an increase on the breakout.
facts.claim: Zanger: volume contracts in the pause and rises on the breakout.

facts.quote: A minor reversal down in a bull trend. Traders expect the bull trend to resume.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag is any minor reversal down in a bull trend.

facts.quote: It can be as brief as one sideways bar or it can retrace most of the most recent leg up.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag can be one bar or retrace most of the last leg.

facts.quote: Most truly sound patterns consolidate a minimum of seven to eight weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: most sound bases consolidate at least seven to eight weeks; it lists no ordinary flag.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: The close is above the 200-day simple moving average on every flag session and at the entry.
facts.claim: The close is above the 200-day on every flag session and at the entry.

facts.quote: The 50-day SMA is above the 200-day SMA and higher than it was 10 sessions ago, and the close is above the 50-day.
facts.claim: The 50-day is above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day.

facts.quote: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the A+ case; the second is normal; the third or later flag in one run without a proper base is graded B- or passed.
facts.claim: The first flag after a breakout or a correction is A+; the third or later without a base is B- or a pass.

facts.quote: A flag that forms right after a parabolic burst is treated as extended until the 10-day average catches up: no entry while the flag's closes sit more than 10% above the 10-day SMA.
facts.claim: A flag right after a parabolic burst is extended until the 10-day catches up.

facts.quote: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag; it has broken out (the T3 trigger).
facts.claim: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole has broken out.

facts.quote: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best. Past 20 sessions it is a base, judged as a flat base or a VCP.
facts.claim: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best; past 20 it is a base.

facts.quote: The flag drifts sideways or down: the least-squares slope of the flag's highs is at or below zero. Higher highs and higher lows through the pause is a wedge up, not a flag.
facts.claim: The flag drifts sideways or down; higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: The flag's average daily range (high minus low, as a percent of the close) is smaller than the pole's.
facts.claim: The flag's average daily range is smaller than the pole's.

facts.quote: No flag session closes red with volume of 1.5 times its 50-day average or more. One such day drops the grade; two end the flag.
facts.claim: One heavy red day in the flag drops the grade; two end the flag.

facts.quote: Every flag session closes at or above the rising 21-day EMA. An intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed and is often the buy.
facts.claim: Every flag close holds the rising 21-day EMA; an intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed.

facts.quote: Riding the 9-day or 10-day average through the flag is the A+ version; tagging the 20-day or 21-day EMA and reclaiming it is the A or B version.
facts.claim: Riding the 9 or 10-day through the flag is A+; tagging the 20 or 21-day and reclaiming is A or B.

facts.quote: An inside day or a narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue: it gives a nearer stop.
facts.claim: An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue.

facts.quote: A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only. Set the alert at the level the night before.
facts.claim: A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only; alert set the night before.

facts.quote: The flag's low is the idea's invalidation, not the default stop. It is almost never a 3% stop.
facts.claim: The flag's low is the invalidation, not the default stop.

facts.quote: Before entry: two or more heavy red days in the flag, each on 1.5 times average volume or more. Distribution, not a rest.
facts.claim: Two or more heavy red days in the flag is distribution, not a rest.

facts.quote: Before entry: the pause slopes up (higher highs and higher lows). A wedge up, not a flag.
facts.claim: A pause that slopes up is a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: Before entry: the third flag in a short run without a proper base. Wait for the base.
facts.claim: The third flag in a short run without a base: wait for the base.

facts.quote: After the entry, a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop has normally been hit well before it.
facts.claim: After entry a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop is hit well before.

facts.quote: Measure the pole. A bull flag follows a 20% to 30% run in 20 sessions or fewer; a high tight flag follows a near-double, 90% or more in 40 sessions or fewer, and rests 5 to 30 sessions.
facts.claim: The tell against the high tight flag: measure the pole; the HTF follows a near-double.

facts.quote: Count the sessions since the pole top. A flag is done in 3 to 15 sessions and is a base past 20; a flat base rests at least 25 sessions in a box up to 15% deep
facts.claim: The tell against the flat base: count the sessions; a flat base is a long box with a tapped ceiling.

facts.quote: Look for shrinking pullbacks. A flag is one short drift on lighter volume; a VCP strings two to six pullbacks over 15 sessions or more, each smaller than the last, before its pivot.
facts.claim: The tell against the VCP: a flag is one drift; a VCP strings shrinking pullbacks.

facts.quote: Find the pole. A flag needs a 20% run in the 20 sessions before the rest; a pullback to the 10, 20 or 50-day with no pole is a moving-average pullback, setup 12.
facts.claim: The tell against the moving-average pullback: find the pole; no pole, no flag.

facts.quote: Buying the pole or chasing far above the trigger.
facts.claim: A named mistake: buying the pole or chasing far above the trigger.

facts.quote: Calling a deep, loose, jagged pullback a flag. Bulkowski: a loose flag meanders and looks jagged.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling a deep, loose, jagged pullback a flag.

facts.quote: Using the flag low as the stop when it is 8% to 15% away, then sizing too big or skipping the stop-width check.
facts.claim: A named mistake: the flag low as the stop, then sizing too big.

facts.quote: Sitting in a forever flag with no trigger
facts.claim: A named mistake: sitting in a forever flag with no trigger.

facts.quote: Adding to a flag trade or averaging down.
facts.claim: A named mistake: adding to a flag trade or averaging down.

facts.quote: Expecting the shape alone to pay. Measured, it does not: whatever edge there is comes from the leader, the catalyst, the market and the management.
facts.claim: A named mistake: expecting the shape alone to pay; the edge is the leader, the catalyst, the market and the management.

facts.quote: Reading Brooks's bull flag (any pullback in a bull trend) as this setup. Ours needs a pole.
facts.claim: Brooks's bull flag is any pullback; ours needs a pole.

facts.quote: bf.which_flag: the first flag after a base breakout or a market correction
facts.claim: The A+ row: the first flag after a base breakout or a market correction.

facts.quote: bf.which_flag: the third or later flag
facts.claim: The B- row: the third or later flag.

facts.claim: The B- row: a Yellow market.

facts.quote: bf.market_reading: Red, or Orange unless A+
facts.claim: No trade: Red, or Orange unless A+.

facts.claim: Seven in ten fixed-stop flag entries come back to the stop before 3R; the small stop and the next trigger are the answer.

facts.quote: A pole of 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst, an HVE or an earnings gap, is the A+ pole.
facts.claim: The A+ pole is made fast on a catalyst, such as an earnings gap.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the entry day, or under the prior day's low when that is the planned stop.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the entry day's low, or the prior day's low when that is the plan.

facts.quote: Trail the last third: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, under the 21-day for a steadier one.
facts.claim: Trail the last third on the 10-day or the 21-day.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop. No starter, no adding to a flag trade, no averaging down.
facts.claim: Full size at one price with one stop; no starter, no adds.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. A post-earnings flag is fine.
facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report; a post-earnings flag is fine.

facts.quote: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the best one.
facts.claim: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the best one.

facts.quote: A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up.
facts.claim: A real stop order with the broker; it only moves up.

facts.quote: Time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.
facts.claim: Time stop: under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.

facts.quote: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
facts.claim: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out past 2R.

facts.claim: A named mistake: waiting for a confirmation breakout and getting stopped in the chop below it.

facts.quote: A tidy 5-day, 4.7% pause on 0.75x volume, but the rise before it was 18.2% in 20 sessions. No pole, no flag: a pullback in an uptrend, judged under the moving-average pullback card (setup 12).
facts.claim: META 2025-07-09 near-miss: the rise before the pause was 18.2% in 20 sessions; no pole, no flag; a moving-average pullback.

facts.quote: A 30% pole and a 6.6%-deep pause on 0.81x volume that ran 21 sessions. Past 20 sessions it is a base, judged as a flat base (setup 01) or a Qullamaggie consolidation (setup 18).
facts.claim: AXON 2024-04-04 near-miss: the pause ran 21 sessions; past 20 it is a base.

facts.quote: A 7-day flag only 12.8% under the top on half the pole's volume, but the low gave back 55% of the pole.
facts.claim: DKNG 2021-02-19 near-miss: the low gave back 55% of the pole.

facts.quote: A 7-day pause 10.7% deep after a 58% pole, but its highs rose 5.6% across the pause. Higher highs and higher lows through the rest is a wedge up (bf.inv_wedge_up), not a flag.
facts.claim: BA 2020-12-01 near-miss: the highs rose 5.6% across the pause; a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: Three closed the trigger day at the high and still failed (QCOM, STZ, LLY): a strong close on a light-volume T2 does not make a flag work
facts.claim: Three of the four failures closed the trigger day at the high and still failed; a strong close does not make a flag work.

facts.quote: Five of the ten have a report inside the pole (ISRG, NUS, RARE, AMD, PANW), which fits Bulkowski's earnings-flag observation
facts.claim: Five of the ten examples had a report inside the pole.

facts.quote: Before entry: a close under the 21-day EMA that is not reclaimed the next session.
facts.claim: Before entry, a close under the 21-day EMA that is not reclaimed the next session ends the flag.

facts.quote: A short rest of 3 to 15 sessions that drifts sideways or down, gives back at most half the pole and at most 15% from the pole top
facts.claim: The card: a flag is a rest of 3 to 15 sessions.

facts.quote: A third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top, is the A+ depth.
facts.claim: The A+ depth: a third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top.

facts.quote: After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop.
facts.claim: After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop.

facts.quote: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
facts.claim: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.

walkthroughs.title: SHOP, May 2020: the flag that held the 21-day
steps: SHOP, spring 2020. The stock doubled in 12 days to 66.57, then rested eight sessions, 59.50 to 66.26.
Every close of the flag held the rising 21-day EMA. Volume ran 0.85x the pole's. Above the 50 and 200-day.
2020-05-04: it trades over the prior day's high. Buy at market, 62.80, under the flag's high. Stop 61.65.
Failure mode: the break stalls and rolls back through the entry day's low. Instead it ran to 41.7R.

walkthroughs.title: AMD, August 2018: four quiet days after an earnings gap
steps: AMD, 2018. An earnings-gap pole: 29% in 14 days to 20.28. Then four days, 18.73 to 20.10, on 0.75x volume.
Our kind of flag: short and shallow, the pole on a catalyst. The pause is 7.6% deep.
2018-08-21: the prior day's high breaks. Buy at market, 20.09. Stop a few cents under the low, 19.81, 1.4% away.
A third at 3R, a third at 5R, the rest on the trail. It ran from 20 to 34 in five weeks.

walkthroughs.title: RARE, May 2015: a staircase, one step at a time
steps: RARE, 2015. A 53% pole in 13 days to 85.93, then four days resting at the 10-day EMA, 80.25 to 85.79.
2015-05-27: it trades over the prior day's high before the flag's high breaks. Buy at market, 83.26.
Stop a few cents under the low, 81.18, 2.5% away. Full size at one price, one stop. No starter, no adds.
Then a second leg the same size. You hold what is left on the trail, with no adds on the way.

questions.q: What has to come right before a bull flag?
choices: A sharp, fast run: the pole
A long flat base of many weeks
A gap down on news
A slow grind higher
questions.answer: A sharp, fast run: the pole
questions.why: A sharp, fast run, the pole. Bulkowski: no straight-line run, no flag. ChartSchool wants evidence of a sharp advance on heavy volume.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag. The run is what the rest is resting from.

wrong.A long flat base of many weeks: A base can come before the run, but the flag itself follows the run.
wrong.A gap down on news: That is a break, not a pole. The pole goes up.
wrong.A slow grind higher: A slow grind is not a pole. Bulkowski: the flagpole should be unusually steep.

questions.q: Which way does a bull flag drift while it rests?
choices: Sideways or down against the trend
Up, with higher highs and lows
Straight down to the 200-day
It does not matter; the pole counts
questions.answer: Sideways or down against the trend
questions.why: Sideways or down, against the trend. ChartSchool: a small rectangle sloping against the previous trend. Zanger: lower tops and bottoms, parallel lines.
questions.lesson_line: The flag leans back against the run. Up and to the right is something else.

wrong.Up, with higher highs and lows: Higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag.
wrong.Straight down to the 200-day: That is a correction, not a rest. A flag stays near the top of the pole.
wrong.It does not matter; the pole counts: It matters. Three sources say against the trend; our card says flat or down.

questions.q: The flag stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, or the prior day's low when that was the plan.
questions.why: True. A few cents under the entry day's low, or under the prior day's low when that is the planned stop. Kullamagi: the stop is always the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. The day's low, a few cents under it.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flag is only ours when every flag close sits above the ___-day simple moving average.
questions.why: 200. The close holds the 200-day on every flag session and at the entry. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, every day of the flag. Below it there is no flag to buy.

questions.q: While a flag forms, what does volume usually do?
choices: It dries up below the pole's
It stays as heavy as the pole's
It rises every day
Volume is never read in a flag
questions.answer: It dries up below the pole's
questions.why: It dries up. Zanger: volume generally contracts during the pause. Bulkowski: it trends down 74% of the time before an up breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet in the flag, loud on the break.

wrong.It stays as heavy as the pole's: Heavy volume in the rest is supply, not a rest. The flag should be quieter than the pole.
wrong.It rises every day: Rising volume through the pause is distribution. Our card ends the flag on two heavy red days.
wrong.Volume is never read in a flag: Volume is read twice: quiet in the flag, higher on the break.

questions.q: The flag buy is a market order when the trigger level trades, in regular hours, from an alert set the night before.
questions.why: True. A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only. Set the alert at the level the night before. Entries are market orders; no new buys outside regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Alert tonight, market order tomorrow, regular hours only.

questions.q: Which flag in a run is the one we want most?
choices: First after a breakout or correction
The third, once the trend is well proven
Any; the shape decides
The one with the deepest pullback
questions.answer: First after a breakout or correction
questions.why: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction. That is the A+ case on our card; the second is normal.
questions.lesson_line: First flag, best flag. Each one after it is later in the run.

wrong.The third, once the trend is well proven: By the third flag the run is late. Our card grades it B- or passes.
wrong.Any; the shape decides: The shape is the same every time. Where it sits in the run is not.
wrong.The one with the deepest pullback: Depth is a grade cue, not a reason to prefer a flag. Shallow is the leader's habit.

questions.q: Which stocks make the flags we trade?
choices: Leaders: RS 80 or more, strong group
Laggards that are about to catch up
Any stock that shows the right shape
Only cheap stocks under $10 a share
questions.answer: Leaders: RS 80 or more, strong group
questions.why: Leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in one of the strongest groups. Bonde: flags are the most common continuation patterns on momentum leaders.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the leader's flag. A laggard's flag is just a pause in a laggard.

wrong.Laggards that are about to catch up: A flag is a continuation pattern. It continues what the leader was already doing.
wrong.Any stock that shows the right shape: The shape alone does not pay. The leader, the catalyst and the market do.
wrong.Only cheap stocks under $10 a share: We trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

questions.q: The flag's low is our default stop.
questions.why: False. The flag's low is the idea's invalidation, not the default stop. The stop is a few cents under the entry day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low is where the idea dies. The day's low is where the trade does.

questions.q: The flag's third day trades above the pole's high. What is it now?
choices: A breakout, no longer a flag
Still a flag, now a wedge up
A failed flag
A high tight flag
questions.answer: A breakout, no longer a flag
questions.why: A breakout. A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag; it has broken out. The pole top is the pattern's high.
questions.lesson_line: The pole top is the lid. Above it the rest is over.

wrong.Still a flag, now a wedge up: A wedge up makes higher highs under the pole top. Above the pole top it has broken out.
wrong.A failed flag: Failing means falling through the flag low. Clearing the pole top is the opposite.
wrong.A high tight flag: The name depends on the pole's size, not on clearing the top.

questions.q: Our card wants the 50-day above the 200-day and higher than it was ten sessions ago.
questions.why: True. The 50-day is above the 200-day and higher than ten sessions ago, with the close above the 50-day. Stacked and rising.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's lines point up and stack in order. Check them before the flag.

questions.q: The day before the trigger is an inside day. What does our card call that?
choices: The A+ tightness cue
A warning the flag is dying
A reason to buy the inside day
Nothing; only the pole matters
questions.why: The A+ tightness cue. An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger gives a nearer stop. Bonde: the day before the breakout should be a narrow-range or down day.
questions.lesson_line: A tight day before the trigger is a small stop waiting to be used.

wrong.A warning the flag is dying: A quiet, narrow day is what a healthy rest looks like. Heavy red days are the warning.
wrong.A reason to buy the inside day: The inside day is the tell, not the buy. The trigger still has to trade.
wrong.Nothing; only the pole matters: The pole is the context. The tight day sets the stop.

questions.q: One flag trade: full size at one price with one stop, no starter, no adds, no averaging down.
questions.why: True. The full size at one price with one stop. No starter, no adding to a flag trade, no averaging down.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one size. No starter, no adds.

questions.q: Where does the first third come off a flag trade?
choices: At 3R
After 3 to 5 days
At the measured move
Never; let it run
questions.why: At 3R. The hard rule is a third at 3R, then another third at 5R and the last third on the trail. Kullamagi's own rule, a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, is his, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R. Sell partials into strength.

wrong.After 3 to 5 days: That is Kullamagi's rule. Ours counts in R, not days.
wrong.At the measured move: The measured move is a reference at most, never a sell rule for us.
wrong.Never; let it run: Letting all of it run is how a 5R trade becomes a scratch. Trim a third first.

questions.q: Through the flag the closes ride the 10-day average and never tag the 21-day EMA. Which version is that?
choices: The A+ version
The B- version
Not a flag; it must tag the 21-day
A wedge up
questions.why: The A+ version. Riding the 9 or 10-day through the flag is A+. Tagging the 20 or 21-day EMA and reclaiming it is the A or B version. Kullamagi: price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day.
questions.lesson_line: The closer the rest rides to the fast line, the stronger the hands holding it.

wrong.The B- version: B- is for a loose, jagged rest. Riding the 10-day is the top row.
wrong.Not a flag; it must tag the 21-day: Tagging the 21-day is allowed, not required. The best flags never get there.
wrong.A wedge up: A wedge up is about the highs rising. This is about where the closes rest.

questions.q: Does this rest pass the tightness test?
choices: Yes; smaller bars than the pole
No; a 2.9% range is too shallow
No; four sessions is too short
questions.answer: Yes; smaller bars than the pole
questions.why: Yes. The flag's average daily range is smaller than the pole's. Bulkowski: a tight flag performs better than a loose one; a loose one meanders and looks jagged.
questions.lesson_line: Tight means smaller bars than the run. Jagged means pass.

wrong.No; a 2.9% range is too shallow: Shallow is not a fault. Four sessions in a 2.9% range was the tightest of our ten winners.
wrong.No; four sessions is too short: Four sessions is a normal flag. Eight of our ten examples rested four days.

questions.story: After a 36% pole the stock pauses four sessions in a 2.9% range on half the pole's volume. The pole's bars were far wider.

questions.q: On flag day four price dips under the 21-day EMA at noon and closes back above it. What is that?
choices: Allowed; the close held
The flag is over; stand aside
A heavy red day on volume
A wedge up
questions.why: Allowed. An intraday undercut that closes back above the 21-day EMA is allowed. The close is what counts.
questions.lesson_line: An undercut that closes back above is a shakeout, not a break.

wrong.The flag is over; stand aside: The close is what counts, and it closed back above the line.
wrong.A heavy red day on volume: A heavy red day is a red close on heavy volume. This closed up, back above the EMA.
wrong.A wedge up: A wedge up is a pause whose highs rise. This is one shakeout under a line.

questions.q: A flag entry more than 10% above the 10-day average is still fine if the pole was strong.
questions.why: False. Too stretched to buy: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. A flag right after a parabolic burst waits until the 10-day catches up.
questions.lesson_line: Let the averages catch up. A stretched flag is a chase with a shape.

questions.q: Bought at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 66.25. One R is the fill minus the stop; add three of those to the fill. That was SHOP's first trim level.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: A flag whose pole was an earnings gap is now five sessions old, with the next report months away. Is it ours?
choices: Yes; a post-earnings flag is fine
No; any flag after earnings is banned
Only if the gap was under 4%
questions.answer: Yes; a post-earnings flag is fine
questions.why: Yes. A post-earnings flag is fine; the blackout is the 3 sessions before a report. Five of our ten examples had the report inside the pole.
questions.lesson_line: After the report is where the best poles come from. Before it is where we wait.

wrong.No; any flag after earnings is banned: The ban is on buying in the 3 sessions before a report. After it is allowed.
wrong.Only if the gap was under 4%: The 4% rule is about chasing past the trigger, not about the pole's gap.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A pause that makes higher highs and higher lows is a ___ up, not a flag.
questions.why: Wedge. A pause with higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag. Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms.
questions.lesson_line: Rising highs in the rest means it is wedging up. That is not the pattern.

questions.q: A flag trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: True. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. Sitting in a forever flag with no trigger is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days with nothing to show is an answer. Take the money elsewhere.

questions.q: Buy here?
choices: No; it is 4.8% past the level
Yes; the break is confirmed now
Yes; half size
questions.answer: No; it is 4.8% past the level
questions.why: No. It is 4.8% above the trigger level, past the 4% limit. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point; chasing costs size, not risk.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent past the level, the trade is gone. The next trigger is not.

wrong.Yes; the break is confirmed now: Confirmed is not the question. The fill would sit 4.8% over the level, past the 4% limit.
wrong.Yes; half size: Half size does not fix a chase. The limit is the price, not the shares.

questions.story: Your trigger is the break of yesterday's high at 50.00. By 10:20 the stock is trading 52.40.

questions.q: The lowest low of the 20 sessions before the pole top was 40.00. The pole top is 47.20. How big is the pole, in percent?
questions.why: 18%. The pole top over the low before it, minus one. Kullamagi's big move runs 30% to 100% or more; Bulkowski wants a straight-line run. Measure it before you call it a flag.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole first. The rest only matters if the run was real.

questions.q: Pole low 40.00, pole top 50.00, flag low 44.50. What share of the pole did the flag give back, in percent?
questions.why: 55%. The drop from the pole top to the flag low, divided by the pole's height. DKNG's flag gave back the same 55%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the give-back against the pole, not against the price.

questions.q: Fill 83.26. The entry day's low is 81.23 and the stop sits five cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.5%. A few cents under the day's low, and inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. That was RARE's stop, 81.18.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Is the flag still on?
choices: No; the close was not reclaimed
Yes; the flag low still holds up
Yes; wait one more session
questions.answer: No; the close was not reclaimed
questions.why: No. By our current default, a close under the 21-day EMA that is not reclaimed the next session ends the flag. Day seven closed under it again.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the line that is not reclaimed the next session ends the flag.

wrong.Yes; the flag low still holds up: The flag low is not the test before entry. The rising 21-day EMA is.
wrong.Yes; wait one more session: You waited one session already. Day seven closed under it again.

questions.story: Day six of a flag closes under the rising 21-day EMA. Day seven closes under it again, on average volume.

questions.q: Buy the break today?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
Yes; the flag is perfect, buy it
Yes; but sell before the report
questions.why: No. No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. A perfect flag two days before a report is a flag we watch, not one we buy.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings in two days is a gap you cannot stop. Wait for the other side of it.

wrong.Yes; the flag is perfect, buy it: Perfect does not report earnings. The company does, in two sessions.
wrong.Yes; but sell before the report: Buying to sell in two days is not a flag trade. It is a coin flip with fees.

questions.story: A tight four-day flag after a 40% pole. Today it trades over the prior day's high. The company reports in two sessions.

questions.q: Buy the break, or wait?
choices: Wait for a proper base
Buy; the trend is proven
Buy half size
questions.why: Wait. The third flag in a short run without a proper base is a wait-for-the-base case on our card.
questions.lesson_line: Three flags and no base is a run that needs a rest, not a fourth buy.

wrong.Buy; the trend is proven: Proven and late are the same word here. Our card grades the third flag B- or passes.
wrong.Buy half size: Size does not fix a late flag. The rule is the base, not the shares.

questions.story: The stock is on its third daily flag in four weeks. No base has formed between them. Today it ticks over yesterday's high.

questions.q: Once the flag trade fills, the stop can wait in your head until the first red day.
questions.why: False. A real stop order with the broker, placed at once. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes in with the fill. Your head is not a broker.

questions.q: Bulkowski draws a line on how long a flag can run. Where is it?
choices: Under 3 weeks, else a rectangle
Up to 12 weeks with no real limit
One day only
At least 7 to 8 weeks
questions.why: Under 3 weeks. Bulkowski: flags are short, less than 3 weeks long; patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels. ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks.
questions.lesson_line: A flag is a short rest. Weeks of it is a base with another name.

wrong.Up to 12 weeks with no real limit: ChartSchool stretches the outside to 12 weeks, but even it calls one to four ideal.
wrong.One day only: One sideways bar is Brooks's bull flag, a different idea. Ours rests for days.
wrong.At least 7 to 8 weeks: That is IBD's floor for a sound base. A flag is far shorter.

questions.q: Grade each.
choices: First flag A+; third flag B- or pass
Both A+; the shape is identical
Third flag A+; the trend is proven
questions.answer: First flag A+; third flag B- or pass
questions.why: The first flag A+, the third B- or a pass. The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the A+ row; the third or later flag is the B- row.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, different grade. Count the flags before you count the shares.

wrong.Both A+; the shape is identical: The shape is one row of the grade. Which flag it is sits in another row.
wrong.Third flag A+; the trend is proven: Proven means late. The third flag in one run is the B- row or a pass.

questions.story: Two stocks, the same tight four-day flag. One is the first flag after a base breakout. The other is the third flag in a long run with no base.

questions.q: Which trigger day gets the higher grade?
choices: The 2.1x day closing at the high
The 0.7x day; quiet is better
Equal; the level is all that matters
questions.answer: The 2.1x day closing at the high
questions.why: The 2.1x day closing at the high. Bonde: breakout-day volume should be higher and the stock should close near its high. Zanger: an increase on the breakout. Both grade the day; neither is the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a strong close grade the day up. Quiet and mid-range grade it down.

wrong.The 0.7x day; quiet is better: Quiet belongs inside the flag. The break wants buyers showing up.
wrong.Equal; the level is all that matters: The level is the trigger. The day's volume and close are the grade.

questions.story: Same flag, two trigger days. One trades through on 0.7x its average volume and closes mid-range. The other on 2.1x and closes at the high.

questions.q: Which is the one thing you never do here?
choices: Tighten the stop to fit the size
Take fewer shares than planned
Wait for an inside day to buy in
questions.answer: Tighten the stop to fit the size
questions.why: Never tighten the stop to fit. Stop first; the size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade or wait for a tighter spot.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Take fewer shares than planned: Fewer shares is what a wider stop costs. That is the rule working, not breaking.
wrong.Wait for an inside day to buy in: Waiting for a tighter spot is allowed. An inside day gives a nearer stop.

questions.story: The break fills at 48.60. The honest stop, under the entry day's low, sits 4.6% away. You wanted full size.

questions.q: Buy the break?
choices: No; let the 10-day catch up
Yes; the flag is a textbook one
Yes; a 12% stretch is quite normal
questions.why: No. A flag right after a parabolic burst is extended until the 10-day catches up. No entry while the closes sit more than 10% above the 10-day. QCOM 2019 was a textbook flag after a one-gap pole, and the trigger day was the top.
questions.lesson_line: A pole that was one gap is not a leader's run. Let the average catch up first.

wrong.Yes; the flag is a textbook one: Textbook shape, wrong pole. QCOM looked like this and fell for four weeks from the trigger day.
wrong.Yes; a 12% stretch is quite normal: Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. Twelve is past it.

questions.story: A one-day gap made the whole pole. Five days later a tidy flag sits 12% above the 10-day average and ticks over yesterday's high.

questions.q: A tight flag in a stock that trades $6 million a day. Our rule?
choices: Skip; under $20 million a day
Buy; the shape is what counts
Buy a tenth of the day's volume
questions.why: Skip. Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Thin names are not watched, let alone flagged.

wrong.Buy; the shape is what counts: The shape does not fill your exit. Dollar volume does.
wrong.Buy a tenth of the day's volume: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and this one is not watched at all.

questions.q: Account 60,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 20.09, stop 19.81. How many shares?
questions.why: 1071. Account times risk percent, divided by the fill minus the stop, rounded down. It stays under the position cap. AMD's 1.4% stop set the size, not the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: If a flag trade opens above 3R on the second morning, the first trim is taken at the open.
questions.why: True. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The level came; the time of day does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: A trim level the open jumps past is a trim at the open.

questions.q: What does that day do to the flag?
choices: Drops the grade; a second ends it
Nothing; only break volume counts
Ends the flag at once; it is a sell
questions.answer: Drops the grade; a second ends it
questions.why: Drops the grade. One red close on 1.5 times average volume or more drops the grade; two end the flag. Two or more heavy red days is distribution, not a rest.
questions.lesson_line: One heavy red day is a mark against. Two is supply, and the rest is over.

wrong.Ends the flag at once; it is a sell: One such day drops the grade. The flag ends on the second.
wrong.Nothing; only break volume counts: Volume is read inside the flag too. A heavy red day is sellers, not rest.

questions.story: Day three of the flag closes red on 1.8 times its average volume. Every other day was quiet.

questions.q: What does that close mean?
choices: Idea dead; the stop went long ago
Widen the stop to the flag low
Hold; the pole still counts for it
questions.answer: Idea dead; the stop went long ago
questions.why: The idea is dead. After the entry a close under the flag's low means the idea failed; the stop was hit well before it, at 19.81.
questions.lesson_line: By the time price closes under the flag low you should be long gone.

wrong.Widen the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. The flag low was never the stop; it is the line that says the idea failed.
wrong.Hold; the pole still counts for it: The pole was the past. A close under the flag low says the run is over for now.

questions.story: You bought at 20.09 with the stop at 19.81. Two weeks later the stock closes at 18.50, under the flag's low of 18.73.

questions.q: What changes?
choices: Smaller and fewer; the grade is B-
Nothing; the flag is the flag
No flags at all until it turns Green
questions.answer: Smaller and fewer; the grade is B-
questions.why: Smaller and fewer. Yellow is smaller and fewer on the reading, and a Yellow market is the B- row on our card. Full risk waits for Green.
questions.lesson_line: Yellow means the same flags with less money behind them.

wrong.Nothing; the flag is the flag: The flag is the same. The market reading grades it down and sizes it down.
wrong.No flags at all until it turns Green: No flags at all is Red. Yellow still trades, smaller and fewer.

questions.story: The reading turns Yellow. Your list has three clean first flags at their triggers.

questions.q: The last third of a fast-moving flag trade. What takes it out?
choices: A close under the 10-day
A dip under the flag low
A close under the 50-day
Any red day
questions.why: A close under the 10-day. Trail the 10-day for a fast mover, the 21-day for a steadier one, out on a close below. Kullamagi trails the 10- or 20-day the same way.
questions.lesson_line: The last third rides the line. The close below it is the exit, not a dip under it.

wrong.A dip under the flag low: The flag low is far below the trail line by then. That gives back most of the move.
wrong.A close under the 50-day: The 50-day is the trend's line, not the trail's. The last third is out long before it.
wrong.Any red day: Red days happen on the way to 20R. The close below the average is the rule.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job: a small planned loss
Cost you the run to 50
Nothing; you should have sold the close
questions.answer: Its job: a small planned loss
questions.why: Its job. The stop is the exit. STZ reached 0.85R, hit the stop on day 2, then ran to 50 without us. Seven in ten fixed-stop entries come back to the stop before 3R; the small stop and the next trigger are the answer.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. The next trigger is the answer, not a wider stop.

wrong.Cost you the run to 50: The run came after the stop. A new trigger would have put you back in as a new trade.
wrong.Nothing; you should have sold the close: A close at the high is not a sell. The stop is the exit.

questions.story: A four-day flag 3.1% deep on a quarter of the pole's volume. You buy the break at 44.34, stop 43.55. It reaches 0.85R, then day two's low of 43.07 takes you out.

questions.q: Bought at 48.98, stop 48.29. The stock trades to 52.43. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. Each R is the fill minus the stop. That is where the second third comes off; PANW got there and kept going.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.

questions.q: What is the stop now?
choices: The first 30-minute low, out if past 2R
Still 61.65; sell at the open
No stop; wait for the close
questions.answer: The first 30-minute low, out if past 2R
questions.why: The first 30-minute low of the gap-down day is the new stop. The ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. That is the one exception to a stop that never widens.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes, not a new opinion.

wrong.Still 61.65; sell at the open: The stop was gapped over. The gap rule gives the first 30-minute bar's low as the new one.
wrong.No stop; wait for the close: The close is hours away. The first 30 minutes decide, and past 2R you are out.

questions.story: Your flag long filled at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65. Next morning it opens at 61.10 on sector news.

questions.q: Bull flag or high tight flag?
choices: A high tight flag
A bull flag
A flat base
questions.why: A high tight flag. Measure the pole: a high tight flag follows a near-double; a bull flag follows a smaller run. Bonde names both as the momentum leader's patterns.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. A near-double is the other lesson.

wrong.A bull flag: A 110% run in six weeks is more than a double. That pole belongs to the high tight flag.
wrong.A flat base: Fifteen sessions is too short for a flat base, which rests at least 25.

questions.story: The stock ran 110% in six weeks on a product launch. Now it pauses 15 sessions a little under the high.

questions.q: Bull flag or flat base?
choices: A flat base
A bull flag
A wedge up
questions.why: A flat base. Count the sessions: a flag is a short rest, and Bulkowski calls anything past 3 weeks a rectangle. A long box with a tapped flat ceiling is the flat base lesson.
questions.lesson_line: A rest measured in weeks is a base. Count the sessions before you name it.

wrong.A bull flag: Nine weeks is no flag by anyone's count. Bulkowski: past 3 weeks it is a rectangle.
wrong.A wedge up: A wedge up makes higher highs. This box has a flat top tapped twice.

questions.story: After a 35% run the stock has rested nine weeks in a box 9% deep. The flat top has been tapped twice.

questions.q: Bull flag or VCP?
choices: A VCP
A bull flag
A high tight flag
questions.why: A VCP. Look for shrinking pullbacks. A flag is one short drift on lighter volume. A VCP strings several pullbacks, each smaller than the last, before its pivot.
questions.lesson_line: One drift is a flag. A string of shrinking swings is the VCP lesson.

wrong.A bull flag: Three pullbacks over 30 sessions is not one short drift. That is the volatility contraction pattern.
wrong.A high tight flag: No doubling pole here, and the rest is too long and too structured for a flag.

questions.story: Over 30 sessions the stock makes three pullbacks, each shallower than the last, volume drying on each. The last one is a few percent deep.

questions.q: Which lesson is this?
choices: A moving-average pullback; no pole
A bull flag
A wedge up
questions.why: A moving-average pullback. Find the pole: a pullback to the 10, 20 or 50-day with no pole is setup 12. Bulkowski: no straight-line run, no flag.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no flag. A drift to the 20-day after a grind is a pullback lesson.

wrong.A bull flag: An 8% grind over six weeks is not a steep run. No pole, no flag.
wrong.A wedge up: The drift is down to a line, not up. The missing piece is the run before it.

questions.story: A leader grinds 8% higher over six weeks, then drifts three days down to its 20-day EMA on light volume.

questions.q: What is it now?
choices: A base, not a flag any more
A bull flag, A grade
A failed flag
questions.answer: A base, not a flag any more
questions.why: A base. By our current default a flag rests 15 sessions at most. This pause is 21 sessions old, and Bulkowski says flags run under 3 weeks.
questions.lesson_line: A flag that keeps resting becomes a base. Past 15 sessions, stop calling it a flag.

wrong.A bull flag, A grade: Twenty-one sessions is past our 15-session ceiling and past Bulkowski's 3 weeks.
wrong.A failed flag: Nothing failed. It held 6.6% deep on light volume. It just stopped being a flag and became a base.

questions.story: A 30% pole, then a pause only 6.6% deep on 0.81x the pole's volume. The pause is now 21 sessions old.

questions.q: A flag that closed under its 21-day EMA on two straight sessions can still be bought on the next prior-day-high break.
questions.why: False. Two closes under the 21-day EMA end the flag. The buy needs a flag that is still on; the next one is a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the line twice and the flag is gone. Wait for the next setup, not the next tick.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job; the leader simply failed
Cost you; it needed more room
Nothing; you should have added lower
questions.answer: Its job; the leader simply failed
questions.why: Its job. The trigger day closed at the low of its range, the next session's low took the stop, and the loss was 1.78%. A planned loss is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out for 1.78%. That is the cost of being there for the ones that run.

wrong.Cost you; it needed more room: More room is a bigger loss on the same failed break. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Nothing; you should have added lower: No adding, no averaging down. A failed break is an exit, not a sale.

questions.story: You buy the prior-day-high break at 276.33, stop 271.41. The day closes at the low of its range, 271.99. Next morning the low of 270.60 takes you out.

questions.q: Bought at 66.62, stop 64.78. You sell a third at 72.14. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. TSEM took nine sessions to get there and then ran past 100.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: By our rules, what came off before the stop?
choices: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
Nothing; it never reached 10R
All of it at 3R
questions.answer: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.why: Two thirds banked. A third at 3R, a third at 5R, the stop at breakeven, the last third on the trail. The trims are what you keep when a flag gives it back.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are the part the market cannot take back.

wrong.Nothing; it never reached 10R: Waiting for 10R with nothing banked is how a 6R trade becomes a scratch.
wrong.All of it at 3R: The first trim is a third. The rest rides to 5R and the trail.

questions.story: A four-day flag after a near-vertical pole. You bought at 80.41, stop 78.66. It reached 6R in two weeks, then rolled over to the breakeven stop.

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
Yes; the flag was A+
Yes; move the stop to breakeven first
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.why: No. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 2R the cushion is thinner than the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Five R buys the ticket through earnings. Two R does not.

wrong.Yes; the flag was A+: The grade does not report earnings. The gap can jump any stop.
wrong.Yes; move the stop to breakeven first: A stop cannot catch an overnight gap. Only a 5R cushion can.

questions.story: Your flag long is up 2R and the company reports tomorrow after the close.

questions.q: Brooks's 'bull flag' means any pullback in a bull trend, so it is the same setup as ours.
questions.why: False. Brooks: a minor reversal down in a bull trend, as brief as one bar or most of the last leg. Ours needs a pole. Same name, different idea.
questions.lesson_line: Same words, different pattern. Ours starts with a pole.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the 50-day is under the 200
Take it; price is above the 200-day
Take it; the pole is strong
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the 50-day above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day. A flag in a stock still repairing its averages is not a leader's flag.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines before the flag. Stacked and rising, or pass.

wrong.Take it; price is above the 200-day: Price above the 200 is one line. The 50 under the 200 fails the other.
wrong.Take it; the pole is strong: The pole is the pattern. The averages are the context, and they are out of order.

questions.story: A 40% pole and a tidy five-day flag. Price is above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits under the 200-day after a long decline.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job; the flag was late in the run
Cost you; the pole was 30%
Nothing; the flag never triggered
questions.answer: Its job; the flag was late in the run
questions.why: Its job. LLY's flag came late in a long run, in a stock already extended on the weekly chart. The planned loss was 2.25%. The lesson is which flag, not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop pays for the lesson. The lesson here was the count of flags, not the shape.

wrong.Cost you; the pole was 30%: The pole was fine. The flag was late in a long run, and that is the grade's other row.
wrong.Nothing; the flag never triggered: It triggered at 957.53 and reached 0.56R. The stop then did what stops do.

questions.story: A five-day flag at all-time highs after a 30% pole, late in a long run. You buy at 957.53, stop 935.95. It makes 0.56R and is stopped on day three.

questions.q: A flag in a stock with 2 million shares a day. You can afford 60,000 shares. Our rule?
choices: No more than 20,000 shares
All 60,000; the stop allows it
Buy 60,000 in three pieces
questions.why: No more than 20,000. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. The risk math may allow more; the liquidity rule caps it.
questions.lesson_line: Size is the smaller of what the stop allows and what the stock's volume can carry.

wrong.All 60,000; the stop allows it: The stop sets one cap. One percent of the day's volume sets another, and it is smaller here.
wrong.Buy 60,000 in three pieces: Full size at one price with one stop, and never more than 1% of daily volume.

questions.q: What kind of buy was that?
choices: An early entry on the same setup
A separate setup of its own
A buy that breaks the rules
questions.answer: An early entry on the same setup
questions.why: An early entry on the same setup. By our current default the flag-top break defines the flag. An earlier trigger keeps the same stop rule. BB bought at 80.41, before its 82.12 high broke.
questions.lesson_line: The flag-top break defines the flag. An earlier trigger is the same setup with the same stop rule.

wrong.A separate setup of its own: By our current default it is the same flag with an earlier trigger, not a new setup.
wrong.A buy that breaks the rules: A market order when a trigger level trades is the rule. The prior day's high is a trigger level.

questions.story: Four quiet days on a quarter of the pole's volume. You buy the prior-day-high break at 80.41, stop 78.66. The flag's high of 82.12 is still above you.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market over 66.26; day-low stop; 3R
Limit 64.00; stop 59.50; hold to 10R
Buy the close; stop flag low; 5 days
questions.why: Market as it trades through, a few cents under the entry day's low, a third at 3R. Written tonight, done tomorrow without a debate.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Limit 64.00; stop 59.50; hold to 10R: A limit under the level never fills on the break, and 59.50 is the flag low, not the stop.
wrong.Buy the close; stop flag low; 5 days: The trigger is the trade through, not the close; the flag low is not the stop; days are not R.

questions.story: Eight quiet days under 66.26 after a doubled pole, every close holding the 21-day EMA. You plan tomorrow's buy.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Add; the trend is accelerating
Hold all of it for the measured move
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long, a burst of gaps and expanding bars, is sold into, a judgment call. Kullamagi's stair steps say the next move comes after a rest.
questions.lesson_line: When the whole move happens in three days, that is the strength to sell into.

wrong.Add; the trend is accelerating: No adds, and least of all into a climax. Bursts end.
wrong.Hold all of it for the measured move: The measured move is a reference, never a hold rule. A burst is the time to lighten.

questions.story: Three weeks after your flag buy the stock gaps up three mornings in a row on rising volume. It closes far above its 10-day.

questions.q: After a flag stop-out, you may buy back the next morning if the stock reclaims your fill price.
questions.why: False. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. A reclaimed price is not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out means flat. The next trade needs its own trigger.

questions.q: What does the strong close tell you about this flag's odds?
choices: Little; strong closes failed too
A lot; it almost never fails now
It means move the stop to breakeven
questions.why: Little on its own. Three of our four failures closed the trigger day at the high and still failed. A strong close grades the day; the leader, the market and the stop decide the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A good close is a good grade, not a promise. The stop stays where it is.

wrong.A lot; it almost never fails now: QCOM, STZ and LLY all closed the trigger day at the high and were stopped within days.
wrong.It means move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not on a good first close.

questions.story: Your flag buy closes its first day at the high on below-average volume.

questions.q: What is the better plan?
choices: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
Buy today; use the flag low as the stop
Buy today at half size
questions.answer: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
questions.why: Wait for the tight day. An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger gives a nearer stop. A 4.6% stop today can be a stop inside 3% tomorrow if the day stays tight.
questions.lesson_line: A tighter day is a tighter stop. One more day of patience buys the size.

wrong.Buy today; use the flag low as the stop: The flag low is the invalidation, not the stop. It is almost never a 3% stop.
wrong.Buy today at half size: Fewer shares is allowed, but the stop is still 4.6% wide. The tight day can bring it inside 3%.

questions.story: The flag's wide day four leaves the honest stop 4.6% under the break. The stock looks ready to print a narrow inside day tomorrow.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a prior-day-high break. Did every close of this flag hold the rising 21-day EMA? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; every close held the line
Pass; two closes sat under it
Pass; the pole was too small
questions.answer: Take it; every close held the line
questions.why: Take it. An eight-day flag that held the 21-day EMA on every close, after a doubled pole. It traded over the prior day's high the next session and ran to 41.7R.
questions.lesson_line: The flag that never closes under its fast line is the one worth the alert.

wrong.Pass; two closes sat under it: Look again: every close of the flag sits on or above the 21-day EMA.
wrong.Pass; the pole was too small: The pole was a double in 12 days. Small is not the word.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades over the prior day's high. Is this pause drifting flat or down, or wedging up? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; the highs rose; a wedge up
Take it; the pole was 58%
Take it; it is only 10.7% deep
questions.answer: Pass; the highs rose; a wedge up
questions.why: Pass. The highs rose 5.6% across the pause: higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag. Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms. It was stopped out.
questions.lesson_line: A rest that climbs is not resting. Flat or down is the flag; up is the pass.

wrong.Take it; the pole was 58%: The pole was fine. The pause after it climbed, and a climbing pause is a wedge up.
wrong.Take it; it is only 10.7% deep: Depth is not the fault here. The slope of the highs is.

questions.q: Which stock has the A+ pole on our card?
questions.story: Two stocks pause after a run. Stock A jumped 45% in five sessions on an earnings gap. Stock B drifted up 22% over twenty sessions on no news.
choices: Stock A, fast with a catalyst
Stock B, a slow and steady climb
Both poles grade the same
questions.answer: Stock A, fast with a catalyst
questions.why: Stock A. On our card, the A+ pole is 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst such as an earnings gap.
questions.lesson_line: The A+ pole is big, fast and has a reason.

wrong.Stock B, a slow and steady climb: Stock B is under 30% and had no catalyst. Our card's A+ pole is 30% or more, made fast.
wrong.Both poles grade the same: They do not. Our card's A+ pole is the one made fast on a catalyst.

questions.q: Before the pole, the lowest low was 40.00. What price is 30% above it?
questions.why: 52.00. Add 30% to the low. On our card, a pole of 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst, is the A+ pole.
questions.lesson_line: Know the 30% line before you call a pole A+.

questions.q: Which flag has the A+ depth on our card?
questions.story: Two flags follow strong poles. Flag A gave back 25% of its pole and sits 6% under the top. Flag B gave back 45% and sits 12% under the top.
choices: Flag A, shallow by both measures
Flag B, it has more room to bounce
Both; depth does not change grade
questions.answer: Flag A, shallow by both measures
questions.why: Flag A. Our card's A+ depth cue is a third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top. Flag A fits both.
questions.lesson_line: Our card's A+ depth: a third of the pole or less, within 10% of the top.

wrong.Flag B, it has more room to bounce: Flag B gave back more than a third of the pole and sits more than 10% under the top.
wrong.Both; depth does not change grade: Depth is a grade cue on our card, and the shallow rest is the A+ one.

questions.q: The pole top is 60.00 and the flag low is 56.00. How far under the top is the low, in percent?
questions.why: 6.7%. The top minus the low, divided by the top. Our card's A+ depth cue is 10% or less.
questions.lesson_line: Measure depth from the top, in percent.

questions.q: You would buy at 56.60. The 10-day average is 50.00. How far above the 10-day is the buy, in percent?
questions.why: 13.2%. That is past 10%. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch before you buy. Over 10% above the 10-day, skip.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Skip a long that is more than ___% above its 10-day average.
questions.why: 10. Too stretched to buy: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Over 10% above the 10-day is too stretched. Wait for the averages.

questions.q: Where does the stop go now?
questions.story: You bought a flag break at 20.09 with the stop at 19.81. The stock reaches 3R and you sell the first third.
choices: Up to your entry price, 20.09
Down to 19.50 to give it room
Cancel it; a third is banked
questions.why: Up to your entry. Move the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: At the first trim the stop comes up to your entry.

wrong.Down to 19.50 to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Cancel it; a third is banked: Every position keeps a real stop order with the broker. A banked third does not cancel it.

questions.q: Our plan moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.why: True. The stop goes to breakeven between 2R and 5R, and the first trim is the default moment.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes with the first trim, between 2R and 5R.

questions.q: Is the flag still a buy?
questions.story: A tight flag rests on the 21-day EMA. On two of its days the stock closed red on 1.6 times its 50-day average volume. Today is quiet.
choices: No; that is distribution, not a rest
Yes; the flag held the 21-day EMA
Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags
questions.answer: No; that is distribution, not a rest
questions.why: No. On our card, two or more days like that mean distribution, not a rest. Each is red on 1.5 times average volume or more.
questions.lesson_line: Two heavy red days is selling, not resting.

wrong.Yes; the flag held the 21-day EMA: Holding the 21-day EMA is a separate test. Two heavy red days end the flag anyway.
wrong.Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags: One heavy red day drops the grade. A second one ends the flag.

questions.q: The 50-day average volume is 1,800,000 shares. A red flag day trades 2,700,000. How many times average is that?
questions.why: 1.5 times. That is right on the line: on our card, a red day on 1.5 times average volume or more is heavy.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. 1.5 times or more is heavy.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a flag break two days ago. The stock is down about half an R and your stop has not traded. A post on your feed says the market looks weak.
choices: Hold; the stop is the exit
Sell half now to be safe
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop. Your stop has not traded.
questions.lesson_line: After the entry, the stop is the exit. Not a post, not a hunch.

wrong.Sell half now to be safe: A post is not an exit. The stop is, along with the time stop after 10 trading days under 1R.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
